subject: Business Studies
name: Business Studies, Year 12
about: HSC, Operations, marketing, finance and human resources
syllabus: NSW Business Studies Stage 6 Syllabus (2010), Year 12 (HSC) course, all four topics

points.title: What operations management is
points.brief: Operations is the part of a business that turns inputs into the goods or services it sells. Managing it well lowers costs and lifts quality.

points.title: The strategic role of operations
points.brief: Operations can give a business an edge over competitors through cost leadership (being cheapest) or good and service differentiation (being different or better).

points.title: Goods and services in operations
points.brief: Goods can be stored and made away from customers. Services are usually made and used at the same time, often with the customer present.

points.title: Operations and other parts of the business
points.brief: Operations depends on marketing for demand forecasts, finance for funds and human resources for skilled staff.

points.title: Globalisation and operations
points.brief: Global markets let businesses source inputs and make goods anywhere, and bring competition from around the world.

points.title: Technology in operations
points.brief: Automation, robotics and computer systems speed up production and cut errors, but cost a lot to set up and can replace jobs.

points.title: Quality expectations and cost-based competition
points.brief: Customers expect high quality, while competitors push prices down. Operations must balance the two.

points.title: Government policy and legal regulation
points.brief: Laws on work safety, the environment, consumer protection and industry rules shape how operations are run.

points.title: Environmental sustainability and CSR in operations
points.brief: Cutting waste, emissions and energy use, and treating suppliers and workers fairly, are expected of operations and can also save money.

points.title: Inputs to operations
points.brief: Transformed resources are changed in the process, such as materials and information. Transforming resources do the changing, such as staff, equipment and buildings.

points.title: Transformation processes
points.brief: The steps that turn inputs into outputs. They differ by volume, variety, variation in demand and how visible they are to customers.

points.title: Sequencing and scheduling
points.brief: Putting tasks in order and setting when each happens, using tools such as Gantt charts and critical path analysis.

points.title: Outputs and customer service
points.brief: Outputs are the goods and services made. Customer service and warranties are part of what the customer gets and judges.

points.title: Performance objectives
points.brief: Operations aims for quality, speed, dependability, flexibility, customisation and low cost. Improving one often costs another.

points.title: New product design and development
points.brief: Designing goods and services that customers want and that can be made efficiently helps a business stay ahead of competitors.

points.title: Supply chain management
points.brief: Managing the flow of materials from suppliers to the customer, through logistics, e-commerce and global sourcing.

points.title: Outsourcing in operations
points.brief: Paying another business to do part of the work, such as manufacturing or customer service, to cut costs or get expertise. It reduces control.

points.title: Technology choices
points.brief: Choosing between leading-edge technology, which costs more but may give an advantage, and established technology, which is proven and cheaper.

points.title: Inventory management
points.brief: Holding stock avoids running out but costs money to store. Stock can be valued by first in, first out (FIFO) or last in, first out (LIFO).

points.title: Just in time
points.brief: Materials arrive only as they are needed, which cuts storage costs but leaves the business exposed if a supplier is late.

points.title: Quality management
points.brief: Quality control inspects outputs, quality assurance sets standards for the process, and total quality management makes quality everyone's job.

points.title: Continuous improvement
points.brief: Making many small improvements over time, often from staff suggestions, rather than waiting for big changes.

points.title: Overcoming resistance in operations
points.brief: Changing operations brings financial costs, purchasing costs, retraining and redundancy costs, and staff inertia, which managers must plan for.

points.title: Global operations strategies
points.brief: Global businesses gain from global sourcing, economies of scale, learning from other markets, and research and development.

points.title: What marketing is
points.brief: Marketing is finding out what customers want and getting it to them profitably. It is far more than advertising.

points.title: The strategic role of marketing
points.brief: Marketing links the business to its customers and helps it win and keep them, building sales, market share and profit.

points.title: Approaches to marketing
points.brief: The production approach focuses on making goods, the selling approach on pushing them, and the marketing approach on what customers want.

points.title: Relationship and societal marketing
points.brief: Relationship marketing builds long-term customer loyalty. The societal marketing approach also weighs what is good for society.

points.title: Types of markets
points.brief: Markets can be resource, industrial, intermediate, consumer, mass or niche markets, each needing a different approach.

points.title: Psychological influences on customers
points.brief: Perception, motivation, attitudes and personality shape what customers choose to buy.

points.title: Sociocultural and economic influences on customers
points.brief: Family, friends, social class and culture affect choices, and so do income and the state of the economy.

points.title: Consumer law and marketing
points.brief: Under the Australian Consumer Law, businesses must not make misleading or false claims, must honour consumer guarantees and must not use unfair practices.

points.title: Ethics in marketing
points.brief: Marketers should be truthful, avoid harmful products being promoted to children, compete fairly and never disguise selling as research.

points.title: Situational analysis
points.brief: Looking at where the business stands now, through a SWOT analysis and where its products sit in the product life cycle.

points.title: Market research
points.brief: Collecting data to understand customers and the market. Primary data is gathered first-hand and secondary data already exists.

points.title: Marketing objectives
points.brief: Measurable goals, such as raising market share by 5% in a year, that marketing strategies are designed to meet.

points.title: Identifying target markets
points.brief: Choosing the group of customers the business will aim at, through mass marketing, market segmentation or a niche.

points.title: Implementing and monitoring the plan
points.brief: Putting the marketing plan into action, tracking results against the objectives and changing strategies that are not working.

points.title: Market segmentation
points.brief: Splitting a market into groups by demographics, geography, lifestyle or behaviour, so each can be targeted.

points.title: Differentiation and positioning
points.brief: Making a product stand out from competitors and placing it in customers' minds, for example as the cheapest, the most luxurious or the most reliable.

points.title: The marketing mix
points.brief: The 4Ps, product, price, promotion and place, combined to meet the target market's needs. Services add people, processes and physical evidence.

points.title: Product decisions
points.brief: Decisions about features, quality, branding and packaging. A strong brand builds trust and lets a business charge more.

points.title: Pricing methods
points.brief: Cost-based pricing adds a markup, market-based pricing follows demand, and competition-based pricing follows competitors.

points.title: Pricing strategies
points.brief: Skimming starts high for a new product, penetration starts low to win share, and loss leaders, price points and price bundling draw customers in.

points.title: Price and perceived quality
points.brief: Customers often read a high price as a sign of quality, so cutting a price can harm a premium brand.

points.title: The promotion mix
points.brief: Advertising, personal selling, sales promotions, public relations and social media are used together to reach customers.

points.title: Distribution channels
points.brief: Getting products to customers, directly or through wholesalers and retailers, with intensive, selective or exclusive distribution.

points.title: Physical distribution
points.brief: Transport, warehousing and stock control that move goods to where customers buy them.

points.title: E-marketing
points.brief: Marketing through websites, social media, email and search, which can target customers closely and measure results quickly.

points.title: Global branding
points.brief: Using one brand name, logo and image around the world, which saves money and builds recognition.

points.title: Standardisation and customisation
points.brief: A standardised product is the same everywhere. A customised one is changed for each market's tastes, laws or culture.

points.title: Global pricing and positioning
points.brief: Setting prices across countries, allowing for costs, competition, currency and local incomes, and choosing how to position against local rivals.

points.title: The strategic role of financial management
points.brief: Planning and monitoring a business's money so it has the funds it needs, uses them well and meets its goals.

points.title: Financial objectives
points.brief: Profitability, growth, efficiency, liquidity (paying short-term debts) and solvency (paying long-term debts), which can conflict.

points.title: Short-term and long-term objectives
points.brief: Short-term objectives are tactical and operational, set for a year or less. Long-term ones are strategic, set for several years.

points.title: Finance and other parts of the business
points.brief: Financial decisions affect, and depend on, operations, marketing and human resources.

points.title: Internal sources of finance
points.brief: Money from inside the business, such as the owner's contribution and retained profits. It costs no interest but may be limited.

points.title: Short-term borrowing
points.brief: Overdrafts, commercial bills and factoring, used to fund day-to-day needs. They are quick to arrange but can cost more.

points.title: Long-term borrowing
points.brief: Mortgages, debentures, unsecured notes and leasing fund large purchases over years, with regular interest payments.

points.title: Equity finance
points.brief: Raising money by selling shares, such as ordinary shares on the ASX or to private equity. No repayments, but ownership is shared.

points.title: Debt and equity compared
points.brief: Debt is quicker and keeps control but adds interest and risk. Equity has no repayments but dilutes ownership and profit.

points.title: The matching principle
points.brief: Short-term assets should be funded with short-term finance, and long-term assets with long-term finance.

points.title: Financial institutions
points.brief: Banks, investment banks, finance companies, superannuation funds, life insurers and unit trusts supply finance in different forms.

points.title: The share market
points.brief: The ASX is where companies raise money by issuing shares and where existing shares are traded.

points.title: Government influences on finance
points.brief: ASIC regulates companies and financial markets, and company tax takes a share of profits.

points.title: Global market influences
points.brief: The world economic outlook, the availability of funds and interest rates around the world affect what finance costs and whether it is available.

points.title: The income statement
points.brief: Shows revenue, expenses and profit or loss over a period. Gross profit is sales minus cost of goods sold.

points.title: The balance sheet
points.brief: Shows assets, liabilities and owner's equity at one point in time. Assets = liabilities + owner's equity.

points.title: The cash flow statement
points.brief: Shows cash coming in and going out over a period, from operating, investing and financing activities.

points.title: Budgets
points.brief: Plans of expected income and spending, such as operating, project and financial budgets, used to control the business.

points.title: Limits of financial reports
points.brief: Reports can hide problems through normalised earnings, capitalised expenses, valuing assets and the timing of issues, and may leave out debts.

points.title: Liquidity ratio
points.brief: The current ratio, current assets ÷ current liabilities, shows whether a business can pay its short-term debts. Around 2 to 1 is often seen as healthy.

points.title: Gearing ratio
points.brief: Debt to equity, total liabilities ÷ total equity, shows how much the business relies on borrowed money. High gearing means more risk.

points.title: Profitability ratios
points.brief: Gross profit ratio, net profit ratio and return on owner's equity show how well the business turns sales and investment into profit.

points.title: Efficiency ratios
points.brief: The expense ratio shows costs as a share of sales. Accounts receivable turnover shows how quickly customers pay.

points.title: Comparing ratios
points.brief: A ratio means little alone. Compare it over time, with similar businesses and with the business's own targets.

points.title: Ethics in financial reporting
points.brief: Businesses must report honestly, follow accounting standards and have their accounts audited. Misleading reports break the law and the trust of investors.

points.title: Cash flow management
points.brief: Spreading payments across the year, offering discounts for early payment and using factoring keep enough cash on hand.

points.title: Working capital management
points.brief: Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities. Managing cash, receivables, stock and payables keeps it at a healthy level.

points.title: Leasing and sale and lease back
points.brief: Leasing gives the use of assets without buying them. Sale and lease back sells an asset and rents it back, freeing up cash.

points.title: Profitability management
points.brief: Controlling fixed and variable costs and lifting revenue through marketing and pricing improve profit.

points.title: Exchange rates and international business
points.brief: A rise in the Australian dollar makes exports dearer and imports cheaper, and a fall does the opposite, which changes what overseas sales are worth.

points.title: Hedging and international payments
points.brief: Hedging cuts the risk from currency changes, through derivatives such as forward contracts, swaps and options. Letters of credit and payment in advance make overseas payment safer.

chapters.title: The role of human resource management

points.title: The strategic role of human resource management
points.brief: Managing people so the business has staff with the right skills and motivation to meet its goals.

points.title: Outsourcing human resources
points.brief: Using outside firms for tasks such as payroll, recruitment or training, at home or overseas, which saves costs but reduces control.

points.title: Human resources and other parts of the business
points.brief: Every part of a business depends on its people, so HR decisions affect operations, marketing and finance.

points.title: Stakeholders in the workplace
points.brief: Employers, employees, employer associations, unions, government organisations and society each shape how people are managed.

points.title: Employment contracts
points.brief: Common law contracts, modern awards and enterprise agreements set pay and conditions. The National Employment Standards set the minimum for all.

points.title: Work health and safety law
points.brief: Employers must provide a safe workplace and workers must work safely. Breaches can bring heavy fines.

points.title: Anti-discrimination and equal opportunity
points.brief: Laws ban treating workers unfairly because of sex, race, age, disability or other attributes, in hiring, pay and promotion.

points.title: The Fair Work system
points.brief: The Fair Work Act 2009 sets the rules for employment. The Fair Work Commission sets minimum wages and settles disputes, and the Fair Work Ombudsman enforces the law.

points.title: Economic, social and technological influences
points.brief: The economy, changing work patterns such as part-time and remote work, and new technology all change how people are employed and managed.

points.title: Acquisition
points.brief: Working out what staff are needed, then recruiting and selecting them.

points.title: Development
points.brief: Training and development build staff skills, from induction for new workers to programs for future managers.

points.title: Maintenance
points.brief: Keeping good staff through pay, conditions, a safe workplace and support.

points.title: Separation
points.brief: Staff leave through resignation, retirement, redundancy or dismissal, each with legal and practical steps.

points.title: Leadership style
points.brief: Autocratic, democratic and laissez-faire styles suit different situations and affect how motivated staff are.

points.title: Job design
points.brief: Designing jobs as general or specific tasks, with variety and responsibility, to keep workers engaged.

points.title: Recruitment
points.brief: Finding staff from inside the business, which is cheaper and rewards staff, or from outside, which brings new ideas.

points.title: Training and development
points.brief: On-the-job and off-the-job training improve skills, and development prepares staff for future roles.

points.title: Performance management
points.brief: Setting goals, reviewing work and giving feedback. It can aim to develop staff or to make decisions on pay and promotion.

points.title: Rewards
points.brief: Monetary rewards, such as pay and bonuses, and non-monetary ones, such as flexible hours and recognition, motivate staff. Performance pay links rewards to results.

points.title: Workplace disputes
points.brief: Disputes arise over pay, conditions, safety, job security and management decisions.

points.title: Resolving disputes
points.brief: Negotiation, mediation and grievance procedures settle most disputes. The Fair Work Commission can conciliate or arbitrate when they cannot.

points.title: Corporate culture
points.brief: The shared values and behaviours in a business. A positive culture lifts morale and keeps staff.

points.title: Measuring human resource effectiveness
points.brief: Staff turnover, absenteeism, accidents, levels of disputes, benchmarking and worker satisfaction surveys show how well people are being managed.
